content:
The [Case Converter](/case-converter) is a free online tool on CalcHub. Every case at once — UPPER, lower, Title, Sentence, camelCase, snake_case and kebab-case. Enter your text to convert and the result appears straight away — no account or download needed. Because it runs entirely in your browser, the values you type never leave your device, and you can use it as often as you like.

Convert any text into every common case at once: UPPERCASE, lowercase, Title Case, Sentence case, camelCase, PascalCase, snake_case and kebab-case. Paste a heading, a variable name or a paragraph and see all eight versions side by side, then copy the one you need. Title Case follows the usual style-guide rule of leaving small words (a, an, the, and, of, in) lowercase unless they start or end the title. Programmers use camelCase and snake_case for variable names, kebab-case for URLs and CSS classes, and PascalCase for class names.

## How to use the Case Converter

Start by typing or pasting your text to convert. The result updates as you type, so adjust any value and watch the answer change. If the answer is not what you expected, check the value you entered first — a missing digit or a wrong unit is the usual cause. The steps below walk through each input in order.

1. Paste or type the text you want to convert.
2. Read all eight case versions at once — no mode to pick.
3. Copy the version you need: click a result to copy it.

## Formula

Each case is a different rule applied to the same words: UPPER uppercases everything, Title capitalises each significant word, camelCase joins words with each new word capitalised, snake_case joins with underscores, kebab-case with hyphens.

That is the standard formula for this calculation, and it is the same one the [Case Converter](/case-converter) applies to the values you enter. You can work it out by hand, but the calculator is faster when you want to try several values, and it removes the risk of a slip in the arithmetic.

## Worked example

Here is a typical example. “hello world, this is a Test” becomes HELLO WORLD, THIS IS A TEST in upper, Hello World, This Is a Test in Title Case, helloWorldThisIsATest in camelCase, hello_world_this_is_a_test in snake_case and hello-world-this-is-a-test in kebab-case. Try the same figures in the [Case Converter](/case-converter) and you will get the same result — then change one value at a time to see how the answer moves.

## What the result shows

With the default values (Text to convert: hello world, this is a Test), the [Case Converter](/case-converter) returns UPPERCASE: HELLO WORLD, THIS IS A TEST, lowercase: hello world, this is a test, Title Case: Hello World, This Is a Test, Sentence case: Hello world, this is a test, camelCase: helloWorldThisIsATest, PascalCase: HelloWorldThisIsATest, snake_case: hello_world_this_is_a_test, kebab-case: hello-world-this-is-a-test, Words: 6. The first figure is the headline result, and the rest break it down so you can see how the total is made up. If you want to compare with a related calculation, the [Word Counter](/word-counter) is worth a look before you finish.

## Which case for what

UPPERCASE shouts — use it sparingly, for short labels and warnings. Title Case is for headings and book titles. Sentence case is for ordinary prose and most user-interface text. In code, JavaScript and Java use camelCase for variables, Python and Rust use snake_case, URLs and CSS classes use kebab-case, and class names in most languages use PascalCase. Picking the wrong one is a style error, not a bug — but it marks the text as careless.

## How Title Case treats small words

Style guides (Chicago, AP) leave short articles, conjunctions and prepositions lowercase inside a title — a, an, the, and, but, or, for, nor, on, at, to, by, of, in, with, as — unless they are the first or last word. So 'The Lord of the Rings' capitalises The at the start but not of or the inside. This converter follows that rule.

## Tips

A few things worth knowing before you rely on the result — most of them are about the numbers you put in, rather than the tool itself:

- For code, convert once and copy the exact form your language expects — camelCase in JavaScript, snake_case in Python.
- Title Case keeps small words lowercase inside the title — that is correct, not a bug.
- Kebab-case is the safe choice for URLs and file names: no spaces, no capitals, no ambiguity.

## Frequently asked questions

### What is camelCase?

Words joined with no spaces, each new word capitalised: helloWorldThisIsATest. It is the standard for variable and function names in JavaScript and Java. Try it with your own numbers in the [Case Converter](/case-converter) — the result updates as you type, so you can test a few scenarios in seconds.

### What is the difference between snake_case and kebab-case?

Both join words without spaces: snake_case uses underscores (hello_world), kebab-case uses hyphens (hello-world). Python uses snake_case; URLs and CSS use kebab-case. Try it with your own numbers in the [Case Converter](/case-converter) — the result updates as you type, so you can test a few scenarios in seconds.

### When should I use Title Case?

For headings, book and article titles, and proper names. Small words like a, the and of stay lowercase inside the title unless they start or end it. Try it with your own numbers in the [Case Converter](/case-converter) — the result updates as you type, so you can test a few scenarios in seconds.
